## What the source is

This is the GDPval paper (OpenAI, arXiv:2510.04374, Oct 2025). The "failure" under analysis is not a single logged trajectory but the paper's **aggregate failure-mode analysis of GPT-5 (high reasoning effort)** as presented in §3.3–3.4 and Appendix A.3, with supporting detail in §A.2.6–A.2.7. I'll narrate it as the lifecycle of a GPT-5 deliverable on a GDPval task, sticking to the facts the paper reports.

## The task setup the agent faced

- **GDPval tasks** are drawn from real work products created by industry professionals (avg. 14 years' experience) across 44 occupations in the 9 largest U.S. GDP sectors. Each task is a request (often with reference files) plus an expected deliverable / work product.
- Tasks are **multi-format and multi-modal**: deliverables include spreadsheets, documents, slide decks (PPTX), PDFs, images, video, audio, CAD. The gold subset references up to 17 files (38 in the full set); 67.7% of tasks require interacting with at least one reference file.
- Tasks are **long-horizon**: average ~7 hours (some up to weeks) of expert work; gold-set average completion time 9.49 hrs, average dollar value ~$398.
- **Grading**: blind pairwise expert comparison — an occupational expert is shown the prompt + reference files and two unlabeled deliverables (model vs. human) and picks the better one, considering both correctness and subjective factors (structure, style, format, aesthetics). Each comparison took experts over an hour.

## The harness given to GPT-5

- GPT-5 (and the other OpenAI models) ran in a **custom harness with the web search tool and the code interpreter tool, with background sampling**.
- Several libraries were **preinstalled in the base image** (footnote references §A.6.4).
- For each prompt, the model was sampled 3 times; 3 human graders rated each sample (9 comparisons per prompt per model across 220 tasks).
- GPT-5 was run at **low, medium, and high reasoning effort**; the agent under analysis is the **high** setting.

## What the agent did and what came out

- GPT-5 high produced deliverables by generating files through the code interpreter (PDFs, PPTX, XLSX, DOCX, etc.) and could search the web.
- **Headline outcome**: GPT-5 high deliverables were graded as good as or better than the human expert deliverable **38.8%** of the time (wins+ties); it lost the remaining majority of pairwise comparisons. It was second only to Claude Opus 4.1 (47.6%). The paper notes GPT-5 excelled on accuracy (correct calculations, following instructions, pure-text outputs) but lagged on aesthetics/formatting of file types like PDF, XLSX, PPT.

## The signals — and the signal the agent did NOT use

This is the crux of §3.4. The agent had multimodal/code-interpreter capability to **render its own output files to images and inspect them before submitting**, but:

- Only **15% of agent runs used their multimodal capabilities to inspect deliverables** before submitting.
- As a result, defects that would have been obvious on visual inspection went out uncorrected.

## Where things went wrong (the failure modes)

From the clustering analysis (§3.3, Fig. 8) and §3.4:

- GPT-5 high lost to humans **mainly because of formatting errors**, despite having the *fewest* instruction-following errors of the models studied. Fig. 8 label prevalence for GPT-5 high: Instruction Following 9%, Formatting 10%, Accuracy 5%.
- The formatting failures were **superficial/obvious**, not deep reasoning errors. Specifically:
  - **Black-square rendering artifacts in generated PDFs — affecting over half of all PDFs GPT-5 produced.**
  - **Egregious formatting errors in PowerPoint files in 86% of cases.**
- The paper also reports (§A.2.6, Fig. 14) that when experts graded the subset of GPT-5 *losses* by severity: 22.9% "model actually better," 47.7% "acceptable but subpar," 26.7% "bad," and 2.7% "catastrophic."
- Separately (§A.2.7), on an "under-contextualized" GDPval variant with deliberately lower-context prompts (~42% the length), GPT-5 performed worse — it "struggled to figure out context" when instructions omitted where to find data, how to approach the problem, or formatting expectations.

## The intervention that confirmed the diagnosis

The authors then ran a prompt-tuning + scaffolding experiment (§3.4, prompt in §A.3):

- **Scaffolding changes**: enabled GET requests in the container; performed **best-of-N sampling (N=4) with a GPT-5 judge** picking the best of four submissions.
- **The corrective prompt (App. A.3)** instructed the agent to, among other things: avoid the U+2011 non-breaking hyphen (use U+002D) and avoid emojis/nonstandard bullets/special characters; keep embedded graphics legible (≥ half page width); **create PDFs with LibreOffice specifically**; use cross-platform fonts (Noto Sans/Serif) or embed fonts; keep deliverable text concise (≤4 sentences) and never link to submitted files; and most prominently a **"Mandatory formatting checks" block**: STEP 1 convert every visual deliverable to per-page PNGs via LibreOffice, STEP 2 display and zoom into the PNGs to look for cut-off/overlapping/distorted/blank/low-contrast content, STEP 3 run programmatic checks (blank pages, overflow, page limits), STEP 4 match deliverables against the prompt's instructions, STEP 5 final pre-submit check; loop steps 1–5 until clean; and append `CONFIDENCE[XX]` (0–100) on the last line.

## Final outcome

The interventions produced large, measurable swings on exactly the failure modes identified:

- **Black-square artifacts in PDFs: fully eliminated** (from affecting >half of PDFs to zero).
- **PowerPoint egregious formatting errors: 86% → 64%.**
- **Multimodal self-inspection of deliverables: 15% → 97%.**
- **Human-preference win rate (wins+ties): 38.8% → 43.1%** (a ~5-point gain), shown in Fig. 9b.

The paper's stated takeaway: many of GPT-5's GDPval losses came from superficial formatting/presentation defects in its own generated files that the agent did not catch because it almost never rendered and visually checked its deliverables before submitting — and these were cheaply recoverable through prompting and scaffolding that forced self-inspection.

Sources:
- [GDPval: Evaluating AI Model Performance on Real-World Economically Valuable Tasks (arXiv:2510.04374)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2510.04374)
